paragraphs.source_en: Esarhaddon was a younger son of Sennacherib, as indicated by his name, which means ‘The god Aššur has given a brother (to the existing siblings)’. He became king of Assyria in 681, despite the fact that he had not been the original crown prince—the heir apparent to the throne, chosen by the king, confirmed by the gods, and appointed in public. When making Esarhaddon crown prince in 683, Sennacherib first had to dismiss his previous choice, heir apparent to the empire for well over a dozen years. This son, Urdu-Mullissi, remained at court, so it is unlikely he had fallen from grace completely, but Sennacherib’s motives are unknown. He did not realize that his decision endangered his life, for Urdu-Mullissi now assembled supporters for a *coup d’état*.

paragraphs.source_en: The conspirators promptly disposed of him and their plot came to fruition: in 681, Urdu-Mullissi and a brother stabbed their father to death. But the aftermath of the regicide saw friction between the conspirators and Urdu-Mullissi’s coronation was delayed. Nineveh was in chaos when Esarhaddon, absent at the time of the assassination, marched on the capital. He managed to drive out the murderers and ascended the throne two months after his father’s death. These events caused a stir all over the ancient world, best illustrated by the Biblical accounts that also report the flight of the murderous princes to Urartu (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38).
